arguments.name: Habermas avoids Christian/non-Christian labels
arguments.conclusion: Habermas does not classify scholars as Christians versus non-Christians but rather as liberal versus conservative on the resurrection.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: He has no right to judge who is a Christian, since God separates wheat from tares.
He uses categories like left/right, conservative/liberal, and scholarly spectrum instead.
Scholars who affirm the resurrection are placed on the right and those who deny it on the left, regardless of self-identification.

st1.quote: I don't say Christian or non-Christian.

st2.quote: I might say left and right. I might say conservative liberal. I might say across the scholarly spectrum.

st3.quote: I have no right to label somebody a Christian or a non-Christian.

st4.quote: if you say you you believe in the resurrection, you pretty much told me you're over on the right

st5.quote: I think it was just one one time you sort of misspoke on a on a podcast and they've taken that and ran with it.

st6.quote: I if I find if you find that anywhere in one of my books, tell me and we'll put it in the list of ARTA to be changed

st7.quote: if you find that anywhere in one of my books, tell me and we'll put it in the list of ARTA to be changed in the next

st8.quote: I might get nailed from the right [clears throat] by not being conservative enough on my view of this or that.

arguments.prior_art: Gary Habermas, The Historical Jesus / Risen Indeed minimal-facts corpus, 1980s-2000s (self-report)

or1.quote: I don't say Christian or non-Christian.
or1.why: A methodological variant of his own prior work rather than a new argument.

or2.quote: I might cite man 60 times and the leading evangelical 22.
or2.why: Adds citation-count evidence not central to prior statements.

or3.quote: I have no right to label somebody a Christian or a non-Christian.
or3.why: No cross-domain bridge; stays within historiography.

or4.quote: I might say left and right.

arguments.weakest_link: The claim that he never uses Christian/non-Christian language rests on his own self-report and memory of his books.
arguments.develop_next: Produce a systematic word-search/count across all four volumes showing the labels actually used.

arguments.name: Habermas cites critics more often than believers
arguments.conclusion: Volume three cites critical scholars more frequently than believing scholars, though not because there are more critical names.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: He counted the citations and found more from critical than believing commentators.
He originally listed liberals first and conservatives second in his source list.
The claim is about frequency of citation, not headcount of scholars.

st1.quote: I have more citations from critical people than I do from believing commentators.

st2.quote: What I meant was I will cite the liberals over and over and over more times than I will cite believers.

st3.quote: I went back and counted volume three. I went all the way through it.

st4.quote: I might cite man 60 times and the leading evangelical 22.

st5.quote: some people are saying >> I looked at your the names and you have more bignamed evangelicals.

st6.quote: I don't know that number because I just wanted to say I just wanted to say to myself, was I am I right in what I recall?

st7.quote: I went back and counted when my volumes were done. I went back and counted volume three. I went all the way through it.

st8.quote: When I did this originally, I listed the liberals first and the conservatives second.

arguments.prior_art: Gary Habermas, The Historical Jesus (post-1975 source surveys), 1980s-2000s

or1.quote: I have more citations from critical people than I do from believing commentators.
or1.why: A variant/extension of his own prior source-survey method.

or2.quote: I went back and counted volume three.
or2.why: Brings a new quantified citation count not in prior work.

or3.quote: I have more citations from critical people than I do from believing commentators.

or4.quote: I might cite man 60 times and the leading evangelical 22.

arguments.develop_next: Publish the actual citation tally per scholar for volume three so the ratio is verifiable.

arguments.name: Charity toward apparent misspeaking
arguments.conclusion: Critics should apply the principle of charity to a single apparent misspeaking rather than treating it as revealing Habermas's real view.
arguments.speaker: Dale (host) and Gary Habermas
premises: Habermas's other interviews consistently avoid the Christian/non-Christian framing.
A charitable reader would examine the full context.
Critics demand multiple clear instances but rely on one cloudy one.

st1.quote: the principle of charity, that's what I call for

st2.quote: all your other interviews you're you're clear. You never you never say that about the non-Christian versus Christian.

st3.quote: I had to. Yeah, because I just wanted to get to the bottom of that when I was um finding out the truth and and you were vindicated, I found.

st4.quote: anyone who's being charitable would look at the full context.

st5.quote: Instead of using one cloudy one, why don't you give me five more clear ones?

st6.quote: I think it was just one one time you sort of misspoke on a on a podcast

st7.quote: if it can be taken either way in context, why don't you find five more places where I said it the the way you're blaming me with?

st8.quote: I had to. Yeah, because I just wanted to get to the bottom of that when I was um finding out the truth

or1.quote: the principle of charity, that's what I call for
or1.why: A distinct methodological/interpretive argument, not a restatement of a prior resurrection argument.

or2.quote: all your other interviews you're you're clear.
or2.why: Uses the corpus of interviews as new evidence.

or3.quote: anyone who's being charitable would look at the full context.

or4.quote: why don't you give me five more clear ones?

arguments.weakest_link: Whether the podcast instance really was a one-off misspeaking is asserted from memory, not from the transcript of that podcast.
arguments.develop_next: Quote the disputed podcast sentence in full context and show it is isolated across the corpus.

arguments.name: Notable scholarly quotes on bodily resurrection
arguments.conclusion: Several prominent scholars, including critics, affirm that Paul and the earliest Christians believed in a bodily resurrection.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: John Cook states Paul saw the same body described in the Gospels.
Dale Allison says Paul meant a bodily resurrection even though Allison is open to non-bodily views.
Tom Wright, Michael Licona, and Robert Gundry make similar strong bodily-resurrection comments.

st1.quote: my thesis is that Paul's view of the resurrection is that he saw the same body as described in the Gospels

st2.quote: Del Allison said Paul believed in bodily resurrection appearance like the gospels do.

st3.quote: He says, "Before you read, I'm going to give you my thesis statement upfront."

st4.quote: The fact that Paul believes in bodily resurrection is very widely taught today.

st5.quote: Boltman can say Paul believed it, but I don't.

st6.quote: The fact that Paul believes in bodily resurrection is very widely taught today.

st7.quote: The fact that Paul believes in bodily resurrection is very widely taught today.

st8.quote: So does Mike Lakona. So does um uh Gundry and his book on S uh Robert Gundry.

arguments.prior_art: N.T. Wright, The Resurrection of the Son of God, 2003; Dale Allison, Resurrecting Jesus, 2005

or1.quote: I believe that the disciples saw Jesus and that he saw them and next Easter will find me in church.
or1.why: A collection/variant of the standard scholarly-quote case rather than a new argument.

or2.quote: John Cook, he's got these two huge memorable volumes
or2.why: Brings Cook, Allison and Gundry quotations as fresh data.

or3.quote: The fact that Paul believes in bodily resurrection is very widely taught today.

or4.quote: He says, "Before you read, I'm going to give you my thesis statement upfront."

arguments.weakest_link: The quotations are paraphrased from memory, and 'Paul believed X' does not establish that X occurred.
arguments.develop_next: Give exact page citations for each quoted scholar and separate 'Paul believed bodily' from 'bodily occurred'.

arguments.name: Presumption of innocence for historical sources
arguments.conclusion: Historical sources should generally be given the benefit of the doubt until shown otherwise, including skeptical sources.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: Outside religion, one normally listens before accusing a source of lying.
Habermas was himself a skeptic for about twenty years, including after his PhD, so he can think as a skeptic.
He has read more material against the resurrection than for it.

st1.quote: I would I would tend to the first view that at any and in any subject way outside of religion, I would tend to be inclined to listen

st2.quote: I was a skeptic for 10 straight years and a bit for 10 more after it off and on.

st3.quote: I've read way more material by unbelievers than I have by believers.

st4.quote: because I've come from that, I can think easier as a skeptic.

st5.quote: but if I know something, especially in this subject, this this area to disagree, um, I'll say so.

st6.quote: I would tend to be inclined to listen and think, "Boy, I've never heard this before." and not say he must be lying to me

st7.quote: It's easier for me to do that.

st8.quote: I've read way more material by unbelievers than I have by believers.

or1.quote: I would tend to be inclined to listen and think, "Boy, I've never heard this before."
or1.why: A general historiographical principle, not a restatement of a prior resurrection argument.

or2.quote: I was a skeptic for 10 straight years
or2.why: Brings autobiographical evidence the prior art does not use.

or3.quote: at any and in any subject way outside of religion
or3.why: Draws an analogy to non-religious practice, but no cross-domain bridge of the kind meant.

or4.quote: I think I tend toward the listening area

arguments.weakest_link: The autobiographical skeptic credentials are asserted, not evidenced, and do not establish the presumption-of-innocence norm.
arguments.develop_next: State the norm precisely (default credulity vs. default skepticism) and give a non-question-begging test for when a source loses the presumption.

arguments.name: Early creedal tradition predates the Gospels
arguments.conclusion: The earliest Christian creeds about Jesus's death and resurrection predate the written Gospels and go back to the 30s AD.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: 1 Thessalonians, commonly dated before 50 AD, assumes its audience already knows the core Christological definitions.
Romans 10:9 and 1 Corinthians 15:3ff preserve early creedal material.
Even the Jesus Seminar holds that the 1 Corinthians 15 creed existed before Paul's conversion.

st1.quote: we know for sure that the a number of the best known creeds have to be pre50

st2.quote: why do you say they have to be before 50? because that's the most common date given to First Thessalonians.

st3.quote: the Jesus seminar took a vote and they say in volume two toward the back, they say that the 1 Corinthians 15 3 and following 3:5 or more verses and Paul's, it's not Paul, but Paul cites a creed.

st4.quote: he never gives definitions. And to a Greek culture, it'd be really iffy to say Lord in Greek and assume they have the same view of Lord as you do.

st5.quote: some of the critics like to say, I never said it was it was early and gave years like that.

st6.quote: I would think plus anywhere in the first 10 is pretty and I can give you a number of guys who will date it between 30.

st7.quote: if you go, okay, Jesus died in 30, and why do you say they have to be before 50? because that's the most common date given to First Thessalonians.

st8.quote: Even the Jesus Seminar holds that the 1 Corinthians 15 creed existed before Paul's conversion.

arguments.prior_art: Gary Habermas, The Historical Jesus (creedal tradition dating), 1980s-2000s; Jesus Seminar, The Acts of Jesus, 1998

or1.quote: we know for sure that the a number of the best known creeds have to be pre50
or1.why: A variant of the standard early-creed dating argument.

or2.quote: the Jesus seminar took a vote and they say in volume two toward the back
or2.why: Uses hostile-source (Jesus Seminar) data as support.

or3.quote: to a Greek culture, it'd be really iffy to say Lord in Greek
or3.why: Linguistic-cultural point, not a cross-domain bridge.

or4.why: Adds a rough chronological calculation, but no formal model.

arguments.weakest_link: The inference from 'Paul assumes his readers know the terms' to 'a fixed creed existed pre-50' is an argument from silence.
arguments.develop_next: Give the exact creedal formulae with their linguistic markers (Aramaic survivals, parallel structure) and a dated external attestation for each.
